interactive.label: Help
interactive.tooltip: Explain what flow maps measures, which settings decide the answer and what to check.

interactive.label: Guide
interactive.tooltip: Walk through the tool step by step; each step waits for you to use the control it points at.

interactive.label: Map flow
interactive.tooltip: Track each tile's correlation peak and read its velocity. Runs in the background.

interactive.label: Load demo
interactive.tooltip: Simulate a scan whose flow profile is known, and load it, so the arrows can be checked against a number. The first time it simulates the scan, which takes about twenty seconds; later it reuses the file.

interactive.label: Export CSV
interactive.tooltip: Write one row per tile: position, velocity and quality.

interactive.label: filename
interactive.tooltip: The acquisition to map: a TIFF stack, or a photon stream (PTU/HT3/…) reconstructed into a confocal scan. It needs at least three frames — a flow map measures what moved *between* frames, so a single image carries no velocity at all. If you have never run one, press ▶ Load demo in the toolbar: it simulates a scan whose flow profile is known, so the arrows can be checked against a number.

interactive.label: Browse
interactive.tooltip: Browse for an image stack or photon-stream file on disk.

interactive.label: Database
interactive.tooltip: Load a dataset registered in the database; the database resolves it to a local file wherever its object store keeps the data.

interactive.label: tile
interactive.tooltip: Side of the sub-region each arrow is computed from — the spatial resolution of the map, and the setting that decides the whole result. Smaller localizes the flow but holds fewer molecules and leaves the peak less room to travel; larger averages distinct flows into one arrow. Several focus waists across is the usual compromise.

interactive.label: n_lags
interactive.tooltip: STICS only: correlate frame i against frames i+0 … i+N-1. The peak has to stay inside its tile over that whole range — its displacement is v × lag × frame time ÷ pixel size. Overshoot and the correlation map, being periodic, wraps the peak round to the other side, where a straight line fits a confident velocity pointing the wrong way; such tiles are refused and counted rather than reported.

interactive.label: distance
interactive.tooltip: Pair correlation only: how far apart the two correlated points are. Too small and the transit time falls below the line period; too large and molecules do not survive the trip, so the peak drowns. Run two distances and check the scaling: a flow peak moves as δ, a diffusive one as δ².

interactive.label: min_quality
interactive.tooltip: Arrows below this are not drawn. It is not cosmetic: peak jitter fitted to a straight line always yields a slope, and a slope is a speed, so an unfiltered map paints a convincing flow field onto a sample that has none. Raise it until a region you know is static goes blank.

interactive.label: pixel_duration_us
interactive.tooltip: Time the beam spends on each pixel. With the line and frame times left at zero they are derived from it, which is exact for a scanner without dead time between lines or frames.

interactive.label: frame_duration_ms
interactive.tooltip: Time between one frame and the next. This is the clock a STICS velocity is measured against, so an inter-frame dead time that is not accounted for scales every arrow. Zero derives it from the dwell.

interactive.label: line_duration_ms
interactive.tooltip: Time between one line and the next; the clock the pair-correlation lags are measured against. Zero derives it from the dwell.

interactive.label: pixel_size_nm
interactive.tooltip: Physical pixel size. Every velocity scales linearly with it, so an uncertain pixel size is an equally uncertain µm/s.

interactive.label: arrow_scale
interactive.tooltip: Multiplies the drawn arrow length. Display only — it never touches the numbers, and the caption under the field says what scale was used.

interactive.label: step
interactive.tooltip: Distance between neighbouring tile origins. Zero uses half a tile, so tiles overlap — which smooths the field without adding information. Set it equal to the tile size for independent tiles.
